Joint model formulation

Source: vignettes/joinme-model.qmd

Overview

This document states the joint model in mathematical form. It is intended for readers who want to understand the model assumptions and the meaning of its parameters before fitting or using the model.

Mathematical formulation

The joint model consists of two linked submodels: a multivariate longitudinal mixed-effects model and a survival model with time-varying covariates defined by the longitudinal process.

Notation

  • N: Number of subjects (i = 1, \dots, N).
  • D: Number of longitudinal markers (d = 1, \dots, D).
  • n_{id}: Number of observations for subject i marker d.
  • (L_i,R_i]: Event-time observation interval for subject i. Right-censored observations are retained as special cases.
  • c_i: Censoring statement: right, exact, left or interval.
  • y_{ijk}: The k-th observation of marker d for subject i at time t_{ijk}.

Longitudinal Submodel

We assume the observed outcomes y_{ijk} follow a distribution from the exponential family (e.g., Gaussian, Student-t) centred at a linear predictor \eta_{ijk}(t).

y_{ijk} \sim \mathcal{D}(\eta_{id}(t_{ijk}), \sigma_y, \nu)

For a skew-Laplace marker, the ancillary quantile parameter satisfies 0<\tau_d<1. It may be estimated, modelled by a distributional regression, or fixed in that marker’s family declaration with jm_family("skew_laplace", tau = value). The fixed value is indexed by marker throughout fitting, pointwise log-likelihood evaluation, and dynamic prediction; \tau_d=0.5 denotes the symmetric Laplace case.

The linear predictor \eta_{id}(t) is decomposed into fixed effects and random effects components. A key feature of JoiNMe is the flexible random effects structure:

\eta_{id}(t) = \mathbf{x}_{id}(t)^\top \boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{z}_{id, id}(t)^\top \mathbf{b}_i + \mathbf{z}_{id, mk}(t)^\top \mathbf{u}_d + \mathbf{z}_{id, idm}(t)^\top \mathbf{w}_{id}

where:

  • \mathbf{x}_{id}(t): Fixed effects design vector (time-varying).
  • \mathbf{b}_i \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma_b): Subject-specific random effects (shared across markers or independent).
  • \mathbf{u}_d \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma_u): Marker-specific random effects (e.g., marker-specific average intercept).
  • \mathbf{w}_{id} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma_w): Subject-marker-specific random effects (the interaction level).

Marker-by-id block. If the marker block omits the inner ( ... | id ) term, then \mathbf{w}_{id} is removed and the marker-by-id block has dimension Q_{idm} = 0. In this case, covariance-style associations (corr, vcov) are not available, because there is no subject-specific marker covariance to model.

This decomposition allows capturing correlations within subjects across markers, within markers across subjects, and the specific deviation of a subject’s trajectory for a specific marker.

Survival Submodel

The hazard function h_i(t) for subject i at time t is modelled as:

h_i(t) = h_0(t) \exp\left( \mathbf{w}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\gamma} + \sum_{k=1}^K g_k(\mathcal{M}_i(t), \boldsymbol{\alpha}_k) \right)

where:

  • h_0(t): Baseline hazard function modelled via spline basis or a user-specifie baseline hazard formula.
  • \mathbf{w}_i: Baseline covariates (baseline age, sex, treatment).
  • \mathcal{M}_i(t) = \{ \eta_{i1}(t), \dots, \eta_{iD}(t), \eta'_{i1}(t), \dots \}: The collection of longitudinal trajectories and their derivatives (slopes) at time t.
  • g_k(\cdot): A functional transformation linking the longitudinal history to the hazard (the “association structure”).

This is a full event-time model with H_i(t)=\int_0^t h_i(u)\,du and S_i(t)=\exp\{-H_i(t)\}. It does not use the Cox partial likelihood. The event contribution is S_i(L_i) for right censoring at L_i, h_i(t_i)S_i(t_i) for an exact event, 1-S_i(R_i) for left censoring, and S_i(L_i)-S_i(R_i) for interval censoring in (L_i,R_i].

For the last case, the common interval-row calculation writes

\log\{S_i(L_i)-S_i(R_i)\} =-H_i(L_i)+ \log\left[1-\exp\{-[H_i(R_i)-H_i(L_i)]\}\right].

The first term represents known survival to the lower inspection limit. It is kept separate so that an inspection time is not mistaken for delayed entry.

The interval2 form requires one event row per subject and presently supports one event type because the cause is not observed within the interval.

Common forms for g_k(\cdot) in JoiNMe are constructed from the following association summaries, each optionally transformed:

  • Current value (CV): the value of the longitudinal linear predictor at time t.
  • Current slope (CS): the derivative of the linear predictor at time t.
  • Correlation association (CORR): a subject-specific, time-constant summary of off-diagonal marker-by-id correlations.
  • Variance-covariance association (VCOV): a subject-specific, time-constant summary of lower-triangular marker-by-id Cholesky-factor features, taken directly from L.

CV is evaluated from the latent trajectory at time t, while CS is its derivative per unit of original study time.

When multiple markers are present, joinme forms marker-average CV and CS components using weights \omega_d (one per marker). These weights apply to marker summaries after transformation and before association scaling. When marker-weight estimation is enabled, a common fitted location and marker-specific departures are added to base weights and the resulting weights are used directly before aggregation.

The common marker-weight location uses marker_weights$intercept in jm_prior(); association coefficients use assoc$slope, and marker-specific departures use the family named by marker_weights$family. Normal, Student-t, Laplace, and regularised horseshoe families are available. The family name "student_t" fits a single degrees-of-freedom value shared by all marker-weight sets under \nu-2\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,0.1); prior_student_t() fixes its degrees of freedom when used for an ordinary prior. The declared association location and scale apply directly on the log-hazard scale, while the common weight mean is on the weight scale. There is no additional unidentified association-scale parameter. Sign constraints required by estimated marker weights are applied after the prior transformation. Covariance-style (corr, vcov) coefficients follow the same rule.

The standardised marker-weight departures and standardised marker random effects retain location zero and scale one by construction. Marker-weight heterogeneity comes directly from the chosen unit-scale departure family. A second marker-weight scale is not fitted because it would compete with the association coefficient multiplying the completed weighted summary.

For covariance regression, standard deviations and off-diagonal partial correlations have independent observed-covariate regressions:

\eta^{sd}_{ir}=\alpha^{sd}_r+x_{sd,i}^\top\beta^{sd}_r+ \lambda_{m(r)}z_{i,m(r)}, \qquad \eta^{corr}_{ih}=\alpha^{corr}_h+x_{corr,i}^\top\beta^{corr}_h+ \lambda_{m(h)}z_{i,m(h)}.

They are declared with formulaVCov = list(sd = ~ ..., corr = ~ ...); one formula is the shared- design shorthand. The SD predictor passes through softplus or exp. The correlation predictor passes through tanh to a row-wise partial correlation. Sequential square-root products form the lower-triangular Cholesky correlation factor K_i, with every row having unit norm. The covariance is then \Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_i)K_iK_i^\top\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_i).

Each \lambda_m is one scalar loading for one packed lower-triangular coordinate. Collectively they form a length-M_{\mathrm{cov}} vector, whose matrix representation is diagonal: \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\lambda)\boldsymbol z_i. They are not a dense loading matrix and do not mix latent coordinate m into any other coordinate. In the ordinary model, \lambda_m is the conditional residual standard deviation of covariance predictor \eta_{im}, before the diagonal link or off-diagonal tanh transformation. It is therefore not itself an entry of the final Cholesky factor, covariance matrix or correlation matrix.

Prediction

For a subject alive and under observation at time t, dynamic survival at a later time u is

S_i(u|t) = \frac{\exp(-\Lambda_i(u))}{\exp(-\Lambda_i(t))}

where \Lambda_i(t) is the cumulative hazard implied by the fitted event and association models.

For an ordered piecewise-linear association, prediction preserves the fitted monotone association curve and its posterior uncertainty.
